utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technicians and the interpreters, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. We are going to continue our case, but, before that, I should like to say something. As we did in previous weeks, more or less mid way through the week, it would be in order to make an assessment of our work. One notes that the Prosecutor has announced 12 witnesses for this week, and we have only heard three of them. This situation draws attention to at least three things: first, the right of the accused to have an expeditious and fair trial must be ensured throughout; secondly, the Aleksovski case has been separated from other trials and, consequently, has its own life and rhythm; and, thirdly, the road to reach the Kaonik prison is very often a long and repetitive one. The Trial Chamber does not wish to bring any pressure to bear on the parties, but simply to organise ourselves and to appeal in favour of the rights of the accused to an expeditious and fair trial. I think that we could proceed at a slightly faster pace. Therefore, the Trial Chamber is concerned by the situation and I think that we should have a status conference next Friday at 2.30 to think over our case with a view to completing it as soon as possible, because, as you know, the Tribunal has other cases that need to be conducted. After having said that, we are going to resume the hearing and, Mr Registrar, can you give us the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. IT-95-14/1, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I turn towards the Prosecutor. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with Ms. Sutherland, Mr Meddegoda and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic. I represent the Defence together with my colleague, attorney Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I give you the floor. I should like to ask both parties whether you are agreeable with the status conference within the framework that we have proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Does your Honour wish me to address those matters that you directed to us in terms of the expedition of the hearing? I would have thought that the progress of this Prosecution has been timely and expeditious and that the evidence has been as finely tailored I think as it can be in the circumstances. There is a great deal of matters that rest upon the Prosecution to prove. The road to Kaonik may be a long one, but it is also one necessary to establish the status of the individuals. It is going to be incumbent upon your Honours eventually to determine whether they were prisoners of war or whether they were civilians. That becomes blurred in the context of these proceedings, because of the nature of the conflict. You have people who were spontaneously taking up arms in order to defend their villages, which puts them into a different category to people who are regular members of the armed forces, and that is a matter that requires differentiation and can only be established by evidence and it is also necessary to have an understanding of the nature of the conflict, otherwise the whole issue of human shields and trench digging becomes meaningless -- so the evidence cannot be limited to just what happened in the Kaonik camp. If a number of charges in the indictment relates to trench digging and human shields, the evidence cannot stop just because someone is told to go out and dig a trench. That is not the end of the matter. Digging a trench may or may not contravene the Geneva Conventions. What contravenes the Geneva Conventions is if they are obliged to dig a trench in the face of danger, and again that is another matter that has to be established by evidence. It is not a straightforward matter; it is a matter of assessment. One has to hear the atmosphere in which these people worked to get an appreciation of whether or not that is what was happening. There are cases where these people were performing work which the Prosecution would not allege at all was in contravention of the Conventions, such as market gardening and so forth around the camp. So, it is because of these issues that that burden is upon the Prosecution to prove -- that may appear to be tedious but nevertheless are necessary. Further, your Honours, the right to an expeditious trial cannot possibly in our respectful submission be interpreted in such a way as to deprive the Prosecution of presenting its case. The accused certainly is entitled to an expeditious trial, and we do all we can to comply with that requirement, but the Prosecution must have the right to present its case, and that is what we are doing and we are endeavouring to do it as expeditiously as possible. With that, your Honour, might the witness be brought in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, perhaps we should also hear the opinion of the Defence on this matter, and specifically regarding the status conference, Mr. Mikulicic. I am sorry, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, the Defence has no objection regarding the proposal of the Trial Chamber for a status conference, which it finds to be absolutely acceptable. As regards the way in which the Prosecution is conducting its case, the Defence would not like to reproach anything at this point in time in view of the fact that the Defence requires reciprocity when its case comes, and the possibility to present its evidence, at least in the same way as the Prosecution has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. The equitable principle will certainly be guaranteed. Mr. Niemann, we can resume with the hearing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yesterday, you took a solemn oath. Are you aware of that today, that you are bound by it today as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, you are going to continue to answer questions which Mr. Niemann is going to put to you. WITNESS M (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness M, yesterday in the course of your evidence you spoke of a first meeting you had with a representative of the Red Cross. I think at that time you said that, at least during part of the time that this representative was there, Mr. Aleksovski was present; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was present when they came and, when we came out of the cell to sit around the table where we had our meals, and when the registration of the prisoners began, then she would ask Mr. Aleksovski to go out so she could talk to us without his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time when Mr. Aleksovski was present with the representative of the Red Cross, did you hear any conversation transpiring between them -- between Mr. Aleksovski and the Red Cross representative about matters pertaining to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not hear anything in particular, because, if they did have a conversation, then they would do so to the side -- slightly away from those present. Until they came the second time, when I know that Ms Beatrice told Aleksovski that, since we had been registered by the Red Cross, that we must not be taken to do labour where we were not safe, and especially not to the front-lines, and to do forced labour such as we had been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when she had told him this, were you taken out again, or did the requirements for you to go to the front-line then cease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, after I heard her say this to him, that we must not be taken there, because we had been registered by the Red Cross, and that whatever happened to us, Mr. Aleksovski would be responsible. After that, that night, we went to a neighbouring village, Strane -- about midnight we went to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember that particular incident when you went to Strane, what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They came about midnight -- some of their soldiers came -- gentlemen from the camp, the guards, Marko Krilic was there, and another guard, and then they took us out of the cells, about 20 of us, and we were taken up to Strane to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion when you had a second meeting with the representative of the International Red Cross at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you meet again with someone? Did the lady from the Red Cross come to the camp another time after the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the first time, I think she came another three times. The first time I complained that I needed to see a doctor, because I had these visible scars on my face from the mistreatment I had been exposed to in the camp, and I asked to see a doctor, because I was feeling pain in my back, in my head and all over my body. She told me that she would pass this on to the prison director and that I would be taken there, but nothing happened. A second time when I complained again, after this second time, Mr. Aleksovski, in the evening, took me to the local clinic in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened -- can you tell us this incident? Did he come into your cell and say anything to you? How was it that he took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had already lost hope that I would be taken to a doctor, so it was well into the night when Mr. Aleksovski came into my cell, and told me to follow him. I went out with him and we went outside the building where the cells were. There were another two prisoners waiting for him. He put us in his own car that he used to drive, and he drove us to the local clinic in Busovaca. When we got there, he told us to wait in the corridor until he went to the doctor's surgery to see something. After that, he came out, a couple of minutes later, and told us to go in one by one. As we entered, the other two went before me -- I was the third -- and, when my turn came, they asked me my name, where I was from, and why I had come. I told them my name, but I changed my surname, because I assumed that my surname could affect my safety, but Aleksovski came up to her and told me to tell her my name and where I came from, and, when the lady doctor asked me where I had pains and what they were due to, I told her that they were pains from the digging, but Aleksovski smiled and said, "Tell the truth. Tell her that there was a dance down there." Then I told her that I had been beaten and that I had pains as a result and the lady who examined me, she had lifted my T-shirt, but she put it back down, saying, "Go away, I will not treat you here. If you get out alive, let them in Zenica treat you." Mr. Aleksovski was present throughout this time and he just laughed at it all. She gave me three pills. I did not know what they were. We went out, we got into the car again. Mr. Aleksovski addressed all three of us then and said, "You see, I took you to the doctor, so do not complain again that I did not take you to see a doctor and that you were not given any medical treatment," though, in my particular case, I was not given any treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any expectation after that as to whether or not you would be required to go trench digging again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not expect to be taken again, because I really was in a terrible condition. I could not hold any tools, I could not bend down properly like I used to be able to, and so I had expected them to spare me at least until my exchange, so I was spared for a day or two, until they needed me again, so again they came for me and I was again taken to dig to Polom, a nearby hill near Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At any stage did you think about or do anything in order to render yourself unable to go trench digging while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, while we were mistreated on a daily basis and constantly and very badly, so I told my colleague who was with me in my cell that he should break my arm so that at least they would not force me to dig and I would not be mistreated on the front-line. So, I thought to myself, if I had to be mistreated in the camp, at least I would not be mistreated on the front-line, because I was constantly mistreated, both in the camp and on the front-line -- not just me but everyone else -- all the other prisoners who were there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time you were in the camp, did you know or come to know a person called Omer, from Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Omer in person. I was with him in cell number 6 for about 15 days, I think. He came later from somewhere -- he was brought in to cell number 6. After that, we were together in cell number 12, and Omer was killed at Polom. I do not know which side killed him -- during forced labour he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "forced labour", what was he doing, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of us wanted to go to the front-line where we were exposed to fire, and nobody wanted to dig trenches for their army. We were forced to do that -- we had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you understand that Omer was involved in trench digging at the time when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he went to dig trenches. He went there repeatedly -- I went with him for three days. After that, I was taken to Kula, and he was taken again -- his group was taken to Polom and when we got back to the camp, I asked my colleague, with whom I was from the first day, I asked where Omer was and he said that Omer had got killed, and that they had brought him, after being killed, to Busovaca -- they had taken him to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask you at this stage, if you would, to look at a photograph that I now show you. If your Honours please, we have a copy, a black and white copy, of this photograph. Might the original colour one be the next exhibit in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might a copy be given out? Could it be put on the ELMO? Just looking at that photograph, do you recognise it, Witness M? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the interior of the building where the cells were, where I was put up for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could that be placed on the overhead projector? Witness M, I would ask you to put it on the screen so we can all see it. When you say that that was the one of the cells that you went to, can you be more precise? When did you go there? Were they the first cells that you went to, or did you go somewhere else first, or can you be more specific about that, explaining what these cells are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the interior of the building where the cells were. This, starting from this side, this is cell number 2, 3, 4 (indicating). Over on the other side is 5, and you cannot see that in the picture, there was the cell where I was. I spent about one month in that cell number 6. This was the toilet for the prisoners, and this was a toilet and a bathroom for the staff -- for the guards and other personnel who were working at the camp and this man here (indicating) is also familiar to me, and I say that this is Marko Krilic, that he is the deputy commander of the camp. I can even recognise him from the back, because I have a very vivid memory of him, and so I recognise him, that it is exactly him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours. You mentioned a moment ago that this was a part of the camp or the cells in which you were for part of the time. Were you in any other part of the camp at any other time during the course of your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was transferred to another hangar, which was up from the hangar where I was originally, and this happened some time in the period between 15 and 20 May 1993, when I was called out among the prisoners and we were in a group of about 50 or 60 persons -- we were called out. We came out in front of the building where the cells were, and we sort of waited there -- some kind of an exchange. Mr. Aleksovski was present there as well as Mr. Zarko -- he supposedly was engaged in this exchange, and then there was some kind of roll call -- they were selecting certain men. In my view, this selection was made according to the age groups and when they finished this process, the older men and the men who were unable to work were put to one side and I was with the other group and we were ordered to go to this other building, to this other hangar, which was up from the building where the cells were, and, when I came to the hangar, I found about 50 to 60 people there. They were in pretty bad shape. They were in 10 times worse condition than the men who were in the prison, because at least in the prison they had these pallets on which one could lie down and get some rest, whereas in this hangar there were some mini pallets where very few people could stay, and the rest were on the floor, which was a concrete floor, or some -- there was less food. It was sort of food fit for dogs. I spent seven days there and I had no container to eat from, so I had to share a container with another one or two persons. Nobody gave me anything to eat from -- some kind of mess tin or anything that I could use for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at Exhibit 85 for me, if you would, which is an exhibit you have looked at before -- perhaps that could be put on the overhead projector -- I think he has seen that. Picking up one of those pens -- the marker pens that are there, are you able to mark with the letter "C" this second hangar that you were taken to on this occasion that the exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it in front of the hangar marked "B" on that map that the people were first assembled for the point of exchange, or was it in front of hangar C, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, part of the people were between hangars marked with "B" and "C". People were sort of lined up and called out. That is where the selection was made. In my view, those who were unable to work, those who were sick, who were older, that is when they were separated out and they were taken to the village of Skradno -- they were not exchanged, they were taken to the village of Skradno -- and myself and another group of men who were taken from this line-up, we were taken back to the building marked with "C" and that is where I spent a week, in this building "C".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken out on this day that this exchange occurred, it was about middle May I think you said that it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you either hoped or expected that you were going to be exchanged yourself on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was called out, I had expected to be exchanged and I sort of rejoiced because I said, "Finally the day has arrived when I will be exchanged." However, all that happened was I was transferred from building B to building C.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know why you were transferred from building B to building C -- do you know why that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a group of HVO soldiers there, and two or three military soldiers and one of those military policemen was a school friend of mine -- his name is Marko Kulic and he was present there, and they were sort of shouting from that position and the director knew that I was from this village, so he said, "Oh, no way is he going to go on that day to be exchanged, because he is from this village" and this was the reason why I was not exchanged at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it is obvious, but just to make sure it is clear for the record, by "director" you mean the accused, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Aleksovski was present almost throughout this time until I was taken to the building C, and I think he even stayed behind after those people were taken away and I was taken to building C -- he remained with these people. He was there the whole time, from the moment when I came in front of the building until I was taken to building C, Mr. Aleksovski was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like you to look at another exhibit, Exhibit 70, and I will ask you if you recognise this exhibit. Again, I would like it placed on the overhead projector. (Handed). Witness M, that is a photograph, but I am wondering, looking at it, whether it is a photograph that appears to be familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is familiar to me. This is the building C where I stayed for seven days. I recognise certain people there, also -- the guard and, again, Mr. Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point to the guard that you recognise as Mr. Krilic -- can you point to him on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This (indicating), this is Mr. Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the gentleman with the back to the photograph, appearing to walk into the door with the number 12 above. Do you recognise anyone else there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, these are some of the prisoners who were staying in this building. This is the interpreter, who was with the International Red Cross. This is one of the guards, named Anto, from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the witness is pointing to the person standing on the platform second from the right of the photograph looking at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see the lady that was from the Red Cross that you have spoken of, who was there with Mr. Aleksovski on the occasions that you mentioned in your evidence -- do you see that lady in the photograph at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not Ms Beatrice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I apologise. Is there anything else about the photograph that you recognise? Do you recognise anyone there who was with you at any stage when you were taken trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this young man with a shopping bag and some kind of paper in his hand (indicating) in jeans and T-shirt -- short-sleeve T-shirt who is stepping out of the building was a young man who dug with me one night -- the night when they -- when they took us to Strane after the visit of the International Red Cross, and this gentleman here, who is walking towards the door (indicating) in this track-suit was also an HVO soldier, and he slept in one of the cells, which was at the entrance and above that cell there was a cross, so he went to the front-line from there, and would come back and slept there. I do not know whether he was in prison there, or whether he was on some other duty, but he brought me food several times into the cell, while I was staying in building B. And also on the second day of my staying in prison, he brought me the food that was later thrown at me, and down here (indicating) are the men from Zepce. This man is from Zepce, and he was helping me -- he had a handkerchief or something and he was dipping it in water and he was putting like a cold compress or something, he was trying to help me to cool off my bruises. This is a man from Vitez (indicating), and then I recognise some of the faces, but I do not know where they are from. They were from different areas. I know them by face, but I do not know exactly from which area each individual was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that is good, thank you. When you were in the hangar that you have marked C, did you become ill at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I came to the hangar which I marked with the letter "C", I suffered a crisis of sorts -- it just came over me and I was very sick. I had terrible pains in the back area, and the gentleman that I showed you, who was from Zepce, he was tending to me. He was dipping his handkerchief in water that was there in the building -- he was putting it on my back to help me. This helped a little and the other prisoners also cheered me up so that I would not give up -- I was in a terrible shape, and regardless of my health condition I was forced to go and dig regardless of this condition -- I had to go to dig and work every day, so that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when you were in the camp, do you remember seeing some prisoners there that were of Arab origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I got there, maybe two or three days later -- in fact, the first couple of days I heard some kind of moans coming from the cells 2, 3, 4 and 5, but I did not know what was going on, until one day I came out to go to the toilet and I could see an Arab, who also had come out to go to the toilet, so this is how I found out that they were there, and then, once, while we were digging in the village of Strane -- this is the first time we went there -- I met a man who went with them, who apparently was their driver. I met this man and he said that there were about 10 or 11 Arabs, and that two Bosnians were also with them. So, this is how I knew that there were some Arabs there, and they had special treatment. They were treated differently than we were. They called them mudjehadeen and they were saying that they were different from us somehow, so they beat them more severely than they did us, and, as far as I know, the UN also came to visit them, so they were exchanged in mid May. That is when the exchange of these Arabs took place, and they left the camp and, as far as I know, they spent about three and a half months in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember at any stage when you were in the cell block which you marked with the letter "A" there being a cell there that had a padlock on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in cell block that you marked "A" -- that is the first cell block that you went into with the individual cells in it -- do you remember one of those cells having a lock on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was cell number 4. It was locked in this period when the first Arabs were exchanged and then another Arab from Syria was brought in and his cell was always padlocked and it would be unlocked only when the food was brought to him and when he was taken out to go to the toilet. For a while I was taking food to this cell, and I saw that the man who was kept there was in a horrible condition, that he had been beaten and mistreated, and I thought it was terrible -- from early May up until my exchange, which was on 19 June 1993, he was beaten up every day, he was abused, and different men took turns in doing these things to him. I recall a detail; when the International Red Cross came to visit us, they went from cell to cell to see who was there. When they came to cell number 4, Mr. Aleksovski was with this gentleman from the Red Cross and we were sitting around the table, where we were taking meals. When the gentleman from the Red Cross asked why this cell was locked, he said that this was some kind of a food storage room and that there was no need for them to enter there -- there was no need for them to see it, so they did not have the key, they could not open it, so they passed that cell and came over to us and talked to us; in other words, they did not want to report him to the International Red Cross. I do not know whether they reported him later, but, while I was there, they were not reporting him there, and he stayed behind me, after I was exchanged. I do not know whether this person survived, whether he came out later, after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Mr. Aleksovski said that it was a food store; did he say whether or not there was anyone in there, or did he just say that, that it was just a food store?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that it was a food storage room and that there was no need for them to open it up, that there was no need to look into that room, that there was no-one there, that there was no need for them to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from being taken to dig trenches, were you required to do any other kind of work around the camp during the time that you were interned there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if we did not go to dig trenches, we would go to do some work privately for the guards -- we did work in their gardens, cut their grass, so those were sort of like household work. It was something that they did not do that we did for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you do this work? Was it in the camp or inside the camp and outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside the camp. We went to Mr. Stipo Andrijasevic to plant potatoes; Mr. Miro, who was also a guard in the camp, we went to cut grass for him; Mr. Anto Cakic, we also went to cut grass; to one of their soldiers we went to plant potatoes and onions and within the compound of the camp we also planted onions and some potatoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 46, please? (Handed). Witness M, would you look at the photograph you are now shown and can you tell me whether you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a building within the compound of the Kaonik centre, which was a former JNA barracks (indicating). This was the building where their army was housed, some kind of interventions platoon that was housed up here on the first floor (indicating). This is the entrance to the building (indicating). To the left is a door leading to their kitchen, where food was prepared for them (indicating) and also here (indicating) there are toilets and bathrooms. I went there a couple of times to clean their kitchen, and to clean their toilets and bathrooms, and I also went upstairs under armed escort of their soldiers to make their beds where they used to sleep and rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And would you mark -- looking again at Exhibit P85, please, which is the other exhibit that we had there a moment ago -- I think it may have gone back -- P85 (Handed). Can you point out on P85 where this particular building is that you have just pointed to in Exhibit 46 -- where is it located? Again, with a marker would you put the letter "D" on it, please? Can you point to it and then put a "D" where this building is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here it is, this is this building (indicating). It is here. This is the building where their army was accommodated (indicating) -- their kitchen (indicating), that was where their army stayed (indicating) and we went there to clean up, and do some other jobs that were not for animals. Everything that was filthy, while they were there and before and after they left, we had to clean up. The toilets were in a terrible condition, and so was their kitchen. We had to scrub it all clean, make it shine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you put a "C" there with a pen for me where that place is -- sorry, "D", I do apologise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from those chores that you had to perform that you have already described, was there ever an occasion when you were required to dig graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went once to dig graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you do that -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the environs of Busovaca in the village of Ravan. They came to fetch us about midnight, they boarded us into a van, 8 of us, and we were driven there to dig two graves, and we dug them during the night, not in day time, but during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at the next photograph I show you -- I have a copy for your Honours and for Mr. Mikulicic -- (Handed). Perhaps that might be given the next number in order?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness M, during the time that you were kept at Kaonik, were you ever required to dig trenches or dig installations for the HVO in the Kaonik area itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day I dug in the Kaonik area at this road -- this is the school building that I went to, the school I went to (indicating) and there is a path (indicating) leading to the school and we dug somewhere here (indicating) some kind of a dugout or trench for the HVO. In my opinion, it was for some kind of Defence -- probably to defend the bridge and this road, because, one could see well from that spot the bridge used to cross the Lasva Valley and go on to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it might be easier if we turn it around that way, it is a bit easier to follow. Looking at this particular photograph, I should have asked you -- it is obviously a photograph of the area that you recognise -- can you point to where the Kaonik camp is itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here it is (indicating). This is the compound of the camp. This is building B (indicating), the one where the cells were; this is the building where there were no cells (indicating) -- it was a hangar in which I spent seven days, and down here (indicating) is the building that I just marked with the letter "D", and this is the road (indicating) leading from building D to building B and C and these are some other buildings (indicating), in some of which of the material was housed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point again, just so we understand it, in relation to the camp, where it was that you dug this particular dugout -- can you point to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicating) just here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you put with the pen a circle, please, at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where the front-lines of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were in relation to that spot that you have marked -- do you have any idea of that? You may not know, but if you do know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were far from this. I do not see much purpose in this dugout. In my personal opinion, they wanted to protect this bridge, at least that is what we gathered from the conversation from the soldiers who were present and who forced us to dig. The HVO lines were far from this in the villages of Strane, Podjele, Loncari, Jelinak and further on, so there was absolutely no front-line there or anything, so I do not see what the purpose of that dugout was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, your Honours. I would ask you to look at a map that I am going to show you, and on that map, I would like you, if you would, to look at it closely, and, if you can, to mark on it the places that you were taken for trench digging during the period of time that you were in the camp at Kaonik. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it is easier for you, you can mark it first like that, because it is easier for you to see, and then you can explain it to us on the screen. So mark it first, if that is easier for you, the places where you went trench digging.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put that on the screen for us now and point to those places and tell us the names of them as you go through them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me start from the first time that I went digging. This is the village of Strane (indicating). This is close to Strane and it is called Komar. Close to Komar in the direction of Loncari and Putis is Bakije. Then I went digging in Loncari. I spent some time here at Kula digging, I also dug at Solakovici but not actually in Solakovici, but away from Solakovici. There is no name here, so that is why I have indicated it with an arrow -- not in Solakovici itself, but close to it, because Solakovici was under the control of the BiH army. I also dug in Carica and at Polom. I dug at another place, but I cannot remember what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that. Do you remember how long you were in the camp at Kaonik, for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period from 19 April until 19 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember now approximately, of that time, how much you were taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of the time I spent at Kaonik, I did not go digging or doing some other forced labour -- perhaps for seven days -- perhaps there were seven days I stayed, and, while I stayed behind, I stayed behind either because I was too beaten up, and because they wanted to beat me up, or there was not any work to do. Otherwise, throughout the period I spent at the Kaonik camp, I was taken to dig trenches and do other forced labour that I was ordered to do. Let me also mention a detail -- I counted once I had on my two palms 56 blisters and when I complained, "I cannot really hold any tools in my hand", I would be given some bandages or some rags to wind them around my palms so as to be able to go digging again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the camp, did you have opportunities to have showers or baths or wash your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not once, from the moment I was captured on 16 April until I left on 19 June 1993 -- not once did I have a bath. They cut my hair once -- I do not know why -- at Kaonik, probably because of lice or some other such reason, because we had no hygiene. We did not even wash or wash our hands, only when we went to the toilet, if you had a chance and if the guard would let you wash your hands and maybe your face and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what about clothing, were you given fresh changes of clothes at any time when you were in the camp, and, if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What clothing I had on me, that was what I took away with me. The vest I wore throughout that time rotted -- it fell apart -- it was rotten, so I threw it away while I was still in the camp. I had some boots that I was given by the guards, because they took my boots -- I was given a pair that were too big for me, and they gave me some kind of trousers, but they took mine -- my military trousers -- and they gave me some kind of civilian trousers and I spent my entire time in the camp wearing this, and that is in those same clothes I left. I never had any change of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At one stage during the course of your evidence you mentioned that you cleaned up the premises of the HVO intervention squad. What do you understand by that -- what does that mean, do you know, "intervention squad" or platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means a unit was ready to intervene in a conflict that may occur, so there would be rapid deployment, like a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the day of your exchange, the day that you were exchanged -- I think you said 19 June 1993 -- did you have a conversation with Mr. Aleksovski on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not I -- I did not talk to him, but, on the day of exchange, when, thank God that it happened, when officials of the Red Cross came to the building, building B, they came and they called out the names of those who were to be exchanged. Then there seemed to be a hitch over one of the soldiers that Mr. Aleksovski did not want to release, so Mr. Aleksovski and Ms Beatrice had a conversation. Ms Beatrice insisted that this man be released, but Aleksovski had his reasons why he did not want to let him go -- Hamdo. Mr. Aleksovski said, "Let us go over here, let us not talk in front of the others, in front of the other prisoners, but let us go to my office to discuss it." 10 or 15 minutes later they came back, and this prisoner was released, the one Mr. Aleksovski did not want to have released, so he was released, too, and then they saw that this man could not walk at all -- he had been beaten up so badly that last morning in the camp, so he came out slowly and we helped him to walk outside the building in front of building B, and then we headed towards building D where the Red Cross buses were waiting, and there was a commission of the HVO and the BiH army. On the way from building B to building D that I marked, Mr. Aleksovski addressed me and my colleague and said, "You will be rewarded if you come back here. You will not get out alive again," but thank God this wish of the gentleman did not come true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The person that you have referred to variously as "the director" and "the commander" and "Mr. Aleksovski", do you believe that you would be able to recognise that person again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please look around the courtroom and if you see that person, would you point to him with your hand, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There he is (indicating), that man who was the Mr. Director in the camp throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we must record that the witness has pointed in the direction of Mr. Aleksovski. Mr. Niemann, do you need much more time to finish with your examination-in-chief, or shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I am finished, but it would be convenient to me if we had our break and I had an opportunity to review -- I think I have completed all the questions I wish to ask, but a break would be convenient for me, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we are going to have a 20-minute break. (10.25am) (A short break) (10.55am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, I assume that you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am Goran Mikulicic, I represent the accused in this matter, and I am going to ask you some questions. Please answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. M, what schools did you finish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Secondary school -- trades school, I am a salesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you speak any foreign languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not fluently, but I speak a little bit of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say "a little bit", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What little I speak, I can comprehend what I am told, but I am not very good with the language so that I could express myself what I am asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, during the events that you described, were you a member of any political Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of a political Party of the Democratic -- Party of Democratic Action in 1991, when the elections took place. However, I did not engage in political activities very actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, are you a religious person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you regularly observe your religious rites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness M, during your testimony, on several occasions you said that you did not give your full name -- your real name, that you concealed your identity at the doctor's in Kaonik, et cetera. Why did you do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because whenever I would mention my last name, I would be mistreated -- I would be beaten and things like that. This happened on several occasions while I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting you, but why was that, can you explain this, can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, but people who beat me could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But people who beat you are not here, so I am asking you. Is your name identical with the name of a village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did something happen in this village which was connected to why you were treated in a way at the mention of your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what could have happened. What I know is the HVO forces attacked our village. I know that they did not manage to take the village, and I assumed that that was why I was beaten, because of my last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, you said that you were a believer, that you observe your religious rite on a regular basis. Did you have an opportunity to do that during your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did this the way I could under the conditions that were available then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anybody prevent you in doing some?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody prevented me, but I hid what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at Bajram, which is your religious holiday, a hodza came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a hodza, a religious priest in the camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was there, I did not see him, and I know hodza from Busovaca from very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, how were the guards dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they have any kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All of them or some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them -- for the most part they had them on their jackets. When they took off their jackets they did not have any insignia on their shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall on the uniform worn by the director, was there any -- were there any insignia there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you sure of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything else on the uniform -- was there any rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see any insignia and I am not familiar with the HVO ranks insignia, either, so I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, during your testimony you said that you were together with your colleague and we will not mention his name, but I think that we all know who it is. You said that you were placed in the same cell together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in the beginning were you two alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, other people were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the beginning. Is it true that, at the very beginning, you were physically abused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that first night I was mistreated. After that first night, my colleague was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to what happened to your colleague. Is it true that you said that you slept all night and the following morning you saw the colleague all bloody in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he told you that he was beaten all night that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you slept in the cell all night that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how big a room it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is two and a half metres by two metres -- something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May I ask the usher's assistance to help me show the witness exhibit number 86? (Handed). Mr. M, who is this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Krilic, deputy commander -- he is the deputy of Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, has this person their back to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By what he is wearing, by how he is built -- I recognise him by his watch, by the short sleeves on his shirt, by the shoes that he is wearing, because I rarely saw him wearing boots -- such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you do not recognise him by his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but I claim that this is this person 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are also saying that you recognise him by his short sleeves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to please show the witness a photograph marked as Exhibit 70? (Handed). Mr. M, during your testimony, you also recognised Marko Krilic in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you show him to us one more time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicates) it is this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is this a person that has the back turned to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the person who is walking in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We do not know this because he is a static photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I know where he is going. Maybe he is going backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a picture from the back, and, in my mind, it is the same person, because I saw this person enough times to recognise him, whichever way he is turned and I know him well enough, and he is vivid enough in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that you cannot see his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that I do not see his face, I can recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, you have extraordinary ability.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, can you show me -- Mr. Usher, can you just leave that photograph there for a moment? Mr. M, could you please focus on the person standing on the platform second to the right, who is this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one of the guards in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you see an insignia on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not. He is wearing -- he is a sort of sloppy soldier. He does not look like a soldier. He is all unbuttoned and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. M, -- Mr. Usher, we have no further need for this photograph, I thank you. Mr. M, you described your encounters with the Red Cross official?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In which way did you contact her -- directly, or through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In which way did she communicate with the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, is your knowledge -- let me first ask you, what language did the Red Cross official use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is your knowledge of English sufficient to understand what she was saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I did not speak enough English to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that you stated previously during your testimony that she was saying something to Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through an interpreter, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that when they spoke they pulled aside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went -- they pulled back so that they would not be behind our backs, but on the other side of the table where we were sitting to be registered and to send messages to our next of kin that we were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, you said that you were taken to see a physician in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were there with another two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of these two persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would not like to reveal their identity. I think that their names are in the statement, and they are from the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, I would like to ask you to write down their names on a piece of paper and then we will show this piece of paper to the Prosecution and then enter it into evidence. Is the Prosecution agreeable to this approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (Witness writes on piece of paper)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, the two persons whose names will go unmentioned, in respect of their identity, what kind of injuries did they have, why did they see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know -- they had certain painful areas in the back. I did not enter into the examination room together with them. We walked in one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were you transported from Kaonik to the doctor in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksovski took us there in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any guards with you as escorts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it was the three of you, the three prisoners, and Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you came to the clinic, you said that you entered the physician's office one by one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When one of the three of you entered, where were the other two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in the hallway -- we were there right next to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you under any kind of guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, you described what kind of medical treatment you received in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You described how during your entire stay in Kaonik you spent a total of seven days there, and the rest out working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- not working entirely. I would be taken there and back, but it was only seven days that I did not leave the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. M, you described all the medical complaints that you suffered through that. When you were released, did you go to see a physician in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was released in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, my question is, did you go to see a physician once you arrived in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question -- I did not go to see a physician, because, with the Red Cross card, I could not prove my identity in order to get medical treatment; in other words, I could -- all my personal documents were taken away from me, so that I could not get any treatment in Zenica. I had to have other documents issued -- replacement documents, and I was born in the municipality of Busovaca, and I had to go there to have my documents reissued, which was impossible, so I gave up on getting medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, that you wanted to see a physician, and you were turned down, or you did not go there at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain -- when I arrived in Zenica, people who had been beaten, who had medical problems, were selected and, since I had no personal hygiene, I never bathed during my stay in Kaonik, I first insisted to go to our family so that we would clean ourselves and then go to see a doctor and two or three days later I went to the doctor's with this Red Cross ID and I could not receive any treatment -- the conditions in our country at that time were very different than they are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing in re-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the exhibit is number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D4 of the Defence and I suppose that there is a request for it to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was implicit and the Chamber has granted admission.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So the number is D4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness M, the Trial Chamber has no further questions for you. Therefore, you have completed your testimony. The International Criminal Tribunal wishes to thank you very much for coming, and wishes you a safe journey to your country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I ask the last exhibit be admitted under seal, if your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank my learned friend -- that should have been my proposal, but I forgot to -- omitted to mention it -- of course I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, are you going to request protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. This application will be made by my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, who will be taking this witness through his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next Prosecution witness we wish to call is witness number 5 in paragraph 4 of the motion dated 20 March 1998, and in respect of that witness, too, your Honours, I am making an application on his behalf seeking protective measures. I am seeking that the witness be assigned a pseudonym and, also, that the image of his face be distorted during the course of his testimony. If your Honours are inclined to grant the application, the witness may be assigned pseudonym N -- he will be known as Witness N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we will take the measures that we took for the previous witness. Are the technicians ready for that? I think that we can have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I am calling Witness N, your Honour. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir, do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please read the solemn declaration that the usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated. Will you please approach the table a little bit to be closer to the microphones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are going to answer questions which the Prosecutor, Mr. Meddegoda is going to put to you, please. WITNESS N

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, their Honours have been pleased to grant protective measures, therefore you will be known throughout the course of your testimony as Witness N. Before I start, may I ask you to read the name written on the piece of paper and would you confirm whether that is your name or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That may be shown to my learned friend and also I tender that document under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you are Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, I take you -- could you state what your age is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, I take you back to the events of January 1993. Do you remember the day when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 25 January, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And it was 25 January in which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The year was 1992 -- 25 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Is it 1992 or 1993 -- which year were you arrested -- 25 January 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25 January 1993 -- in 1991 it started but on 25 January 1993 is when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you at the time you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my house with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And who arrested you when you were in your house with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers of the HVO army arrested me and among them were those with the HV insignia of the Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what these soldiers were dressed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers were dressed in camouflage uniforms, they had caps on top of them, they had helmets and they were fully equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying they were "fully equipped"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had weapons, they were dressed completely, they wore stockings over their faces, they had helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were any of these soldiers carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had long barrelled weapons, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you recall about how many soldiers were there at the time you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say certainly, but there were definitely more than 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought out in front of the house, we were driven together down the street with the other neighbours with children. The houses in the surrounding hills were on fire, there were soldiers walking around in the streets carrying weapons. It was an event that was hard to describe. At times, we could not -- why, how? We started towards the centre of town where a bus was waiting. As we were approaching buses we saw their soldiers looting Muslim businesses or stores, and on one side there were kiosks and the women and children had been separated out, and we were ordered to board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After being ordered to board the bus, were you driven in the bus in any direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken -- after the bus was full and it was packed -- it was overcrowded -- and we were then taken in the direction of Kaonik to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened upon arrival at the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought there, we passed a building which was past a gate and this building was where the Croat soldiers were staying. We passed that building, and a short distance later the bus came to a stop, we got off and we were taken -- the HVO soldiers were behind us and we were taken to a hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, would the usher please show -- I am tendering an aerial photograph of the camp which has already been tendered. May the usher be asked to hand over a copy to the witness, and there are copies each for your Honours and for Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you carefully look at that aerial photograph that has been given to you, and, placing it on the ELMO that is beside you, could you point out the building to which you were brought in Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were brought to this building (indicates). This was a hangar, the one we were brought to the first time, this building here, and this was the prison (indicates) with cells, this other building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you please, using one of the markers by your side, mark with the letter "A" the hangar building that you were first brought to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You also said the building next to that was the building with the cells; could you please mark that building with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Upon being brought to that hangar building, do you remember what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all crowded into a group. There were other people there too, I do not know exactly how many, and Mr. Aleksovski came -- that gentleman (indicating) and he issued orders -- whether we had anything on us, any hard objects or anything in their pockets, they had to empty all those things out, and the order was given that all of us should turn against the wall, to face the wall. We did as we were ordered. We faced the wall and raised our hands against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you faced the wall, raising your hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This did not last long -- a couple of soldiers approached and they searched us by hand, to make sure that there was nothing left in the way of arms or knives or anything like that. As they did not find anything on any one of us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you said when you were brought in, Zlatko Aleksovski was present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was dressed in, Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in camouflage uniform. He was heavier, he was of medium height, he was more fair -- his hair was fair, though he has lost weight now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did he address the prisoners who were brought into the hangar building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said, "I am the director of the Kaonik prison, and you are now my responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Aleksovski, were there other camp officials present at the time you were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- only I do not recall their names, who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what were those camp officials dressed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I will not need the photograph any more. Witness, could you tell this court what happened after you were searched inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After having been searched in the hangar, the order was given, after the search was made and our things put aside, to turn around again and again we formed a group. It was almost dark and there was no light inside. We were told that we would stay there under his orders, and that evening there were pallets that we would lie on. Those of us who did not have pallets -- these pallets were wide -- one pallet was for two people, for two men. Some people had blankets, some did not, but nobody really cared -- we were all in a panic and frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened to you the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, in the afternoon, men were rounded up in that same hangar and the order was that 15 to 20 men should get ready, that is, those whose names were called out from a list, that they would be used as a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were names called out from a list at any point in time that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the names were called out. I do not remember exactly what time it was, but somewhere around 1 or 2 in the afternoon, and we were a human shield until 5 or 6 and the names were called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell the court who called out the names of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names of the prisoners were called out by Marko Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know who Marko Krilic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Krilic was the deputy of the director of the camp, because Marko Krilic introduced himself when we were forced down from Kula and he told us when Aleksovski was absent, that he would stand in for him and carry out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What kind of dress was Marko Krilic dressed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Krilic was also dressed in a camouflage uniform -- he had boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after your names -- was your name called out by Marko Krilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened when your name was called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my name was called out, a bus, a Centrotrans bus was waiting -- the same bus that had brought us to the camp and when the names were read out, Ljubo Brnjic was ordered to tie up the men, and Ljubo Brnjic said that he could not tie up the men whose names had been called out, so Drago Pusic did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember how the men were tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were also dressed in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember how the prisoners were tied by Drago Pusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a white rope and we were ordered to put our hands behind our backs, and he took a white rope, and tied us in groups of five. The whole group numbered 15 men -- the remaining five did not need to go, so just this group of 15 men were tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you were tied up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After being tied up, we were ordered to board the bus with our hands tied behind our backs, one by one to climb up the steps into the bus and to go to the far end of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened after you got into the bus -- after you and the other prisoners who were tied got into the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus set off towards the village of Skradno, but it did not go all the way there -- it stopped at a bus station where there is a kind of widening of the road and we were ordered to get off the bus with our hands still tied and, when we got off the bus, the soldiers were standing behind our backs, and ordered us to move on towards the village of Skradno, so we went along the road and we reached the bridge known as Sendoline Kuce. We passed the bridge and, as soon as we passed the bridge, we were ordered to -- after crossing the bridge -- to spread out towards the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, might the witness be shown the document that I wish to tender at this stage? There is a copy one each for your Honour and one for Mr. Mikulicic and I tender that as the next exhibit in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Meddegoda -- witness, could you put your headphones on your head like this? It would be more comfortable for you I think. Is that not better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
